name: Pseudoceramide

lead: Ceramides make up about half of the lipid "mortar" between skin cells, and help hold in moisture. Pseudoceramides are lab-made molecules designed to act like them in creams and lotions.

The payoff for appearance is skin that is better hydrated and less dry and flaky, which reads as smoother and calmer. Most trials come from Japan and Korea, often in people with atopic dermatitis, and some include hair-growth work.

paras: They are included in moisturisers, often alongside eucalyptus extract or other ingredients, and applied to skin once or twice a day. Trials typically run for weeks.
Topical moisturisers are generally well tolerated. A 2015 safety assessment covers ceramide 3 in cosmetics. People with eczema or allergies read ingredient labels as usual.

chain: Supplements barrier lipids and reduces water loss
Skin looks smoother and less dry
angle.text: Used as a barrier-support ingredient. People with dry, sensitive or eczema-prone skin use such formulas for comfort and a calmer look.

lead: Pseudoceramides are synthetic molecules that imitate ceramides, the waxy lipids that make up about half of the lipid matrix of the skin's outer layer alongside cholesterol and free fatty acids, forming a barrier that limits water loss [1]. Moisturisers use them to supplement the skin's own ceramides so dry or damaged skin looks and feels smoother.

Most human research comes from atopic dermatitis, where ceramide profiles are altered. A trial reported that topical pseudoceramide changed the ceramide profile of atopic skin toward a healthy one [2]; others tested a pseudoceramide and eucalyptus moisturiser in Japanese patients with mild atopic dermatitis [3] and on sweating function [4]. A 2025 randomised trial examined absorption into the stratum corneum, water loss and the ceramide profile [5]. Separate work tested a sphingolipid-mimetic compound for hair growth [6][7].

paras: Natural ceramides consist of sphingosine and a fatty acid, and appear in cosmetics including creams, shampoos and sunscreens [1]. Pseudoceramides are structurally related designs; an investigative-dermatology study characterised emulsions containing pseudoceramide and synthetic ceramide 3 [8].

Randomised and controlled trials have examined pseudoceramide moisturisers in atopic dermatitis, including a Japanese summer study [3], a left-right comparison on sweating in 19 patients [4], and a 2024 review of pseudoceramide plus eucalyptus extract [9]. A clinical trial reported ceramide-profile changes in atopic skin [2], and a 2025 randomised trial studied absorption [5].
In hair, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested a sphingolipid-mimetic compound for hair growth [6], following laboratory work on a ceramide mimetic [7].
A safety and risk assessment of ceramide 3 in cosmetics was published in 2015 [10].
